# Bhesajjakkhandhaka (Kd 6)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* ("The chapter on medicines") is the sixth chapter of the *Mahāvagga* in the Vinaya Piṭaka [Frauwallner 1956]. It regulates monastic health care, allowable medical treatments, and edible medicaments [Wijayaratna 1990]. The narrative opening situates the Buddha's initial allowance of medication during an autumnal illness (*sāradikābādha*) that left the monks emaciated and sickly [Gnanarama 1998]. It formalizes allowances for sick monastics to consume the five basic medicinal tonics (such as ghee and honey) outside the usual mealtime, as well as therapies involving various roots, leaves, fruits, salts, oils, and ointments [Wijayaratna 1990]. The chapter also regulates food preparation and consumption, laying down bans on certain meats and monastic cooking, while granting temporary dispensations regarding the storing and cooking of food during periods of severe famine [Rahula 1978]. Prominent narrative episodes include the miraculous deeds of the monk Pilindavaccha, courtesan Ambapālī's gift of her mango grove, the conversion of general Sīha, and the merchant Meṇḍaka, whose account establishes the "Meṇḍaka allowance" for requisites held in trust by stewards. The text concludes by presenting the four great indicators (*mahāpadesa*) or standards for deciding whether a given practice is permissible [Khemananda 1993].

Curated parallels and cross-traditional evidence show that the chapter corresponds to the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* preserved in the Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mūlasarvāstivāda, and Sarvāstivāda Vinayas in Chinese, Tibetan (*Dulva*), and Sanskrit [Banerjee 1979; Dutt; Frauwallner 1956]. While the legal rules on medicines in the Northern versions closely align with the Pali text, their narrative frameworks diverge substantially, incorporating extensive *buddhāvadāna* cycles that are absent in the Pali recension [Banerjee 1979]. The chapter also shares narrative episodes and discourses with texts across the Pali Canon, including the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16), *Sīhasutta* (AN 8.12), *Sela Sutta* (MN 92 / Snp 3.7), and *Pāṭaligāmiya Sutta* (Ud 8.6). Automated text-reuse analysis in DharmaNexus corroborates these correspondences, showing high segment overlap with DN 16, AN 8, Ud 8.6, and other Khandhaka sections (such as Kd 1, Kd 15, and Kd 16), as well as strong cross-linguistic alignment with Sanskrit fragments of the *Bhaiṣajyavastu*, *Saṅghabhedavastu*, and *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra*, alongside Tibetan Vinaya collections [DharmaNexus]. In the commentarial tradition, the text is discussed in the *Samantapāsādikā*, which adopted a textual sequence differing in certain respects from older strata like the *Sīhaḷamātikāsaṭṭhakathā* and *Mahāpaccarī* [von Hinüber 1996].
